query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a low concentration of a secondary microalloying element (i.e. an additional alloying element that increases the overall mixing entropy without presupposing its specific chemical identity) into phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the resultant amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy/compositionally complex alloys that currently exhibit marginal glass formation with relatively modest thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a minor amount (e.g., a few atomic percent) of an additional alloying element to increase the mixing entropy of the system.
generation.conditions: The effect is expected under processing conditions where the cooling rate is comparable between the modified and baseline alloys, and provided that the added element is introduced at a level low enough to avoid phase separation or formation of crystalline intermetallic compounds.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased effective mixing entropy and a more uniform atomic size distribution that minimizes local lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: The microalloying intervention is postulated to lower the liquid fragility by promoting a more homogeneous liquid structure in the melt prior to vitrification, thereby reducing the critical cooling rate for glass formation and delaying crystallization on heating, which in turn stabilizes the amorphous state.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in liquid fragility, evidenced by a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation, and an increased temperature window between the glass transition and crystallization (improved thermal stability) compared to a similar alloy without the intervention.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys produced without the additional microalloying element, which exhibit standard glass-forming ability and a relatively narrow thermal stability range of the amorphous state.
generation.boundary: This intervention may fail or even be detrimental if the concentration of the secondary element is too high, if its atomic size or bonding characteristics are too dissimilar (resulting in unwanted phase separation), or if it interacts unfavorably with phosphorus.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of the secondary element and its precise identity remain to be determined, and the magnitude of improvements in glass-forming ability and thermal stability may vary depending on the specific alloy system and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of phosphorus-containing high-entropy (or compositionally complex) alloy samples: one set with the low concentration of the additional microalloying element and a control set without it. Use identical melting and cooling procedures to form the amorphous structure. Characterize both sets using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the glass transition and crystallization onset temperatures, as well as critical cooling rate measurements via controlled solidification experiments.
measurements: Critical cooling rate for glass formation
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm amorphous structure
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the additional microalloying element do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in liquid fragility (lower critical cooling rate) and/or an expanded temperature difference between Tg and Tx compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Separating the Role of Mixing‐Entropy on the Dynamics of Glass‐Forming Liquids

Abstract: AbstractWhile the concept of high entropy has gained prominence in materials design, disentangling specific impacts of entropy on material properties from the enthalpy of mixing remains elusive. It is demonstrated that the role of entropy can be distinguished from the dynamics of glass‐forming liquids through micro‐alloying. Based on experiment analysis of 79 compositions, liquid fragility is found to consistently decreases under two conditions: i) when the alloying content x is minimal, irrespective of the elements used; or ii) when increasing the diversity of alloying elements at a constant x, namely the high‐entropy micro‐alloying. These observations are consistent with thermodynamic principles that favor an entropy‐dominated regime over enthalpy. These findings elucidate the subtle impact of mixing entropy on material properties and provide evidence of the entropy nature of glass transition. This research innovates by distinguishing entropy’s impact from enthalpy in materials through micro‐alloying. It finds liquid fragility decreases with minimal alloying content or increased element dive
